decks.title: Real Numbers — Part 1: Prime factorisation, HCF and LCM
goals: Express a composite number as a product of primes using a factor tree or repeated division
State the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic and explain why the factorisation is unique
Find the HCF and LCM of two or three numbers by prime factorisation
Verify HCF × LCM = product for two numbers and know when it fails
Solve word problems on bells, buses, tiles and packing using HCF and LCM

slides.heading: Real Numbers, Part 1: Primes, HCF and LCM
slides.body_md: Every whole number greater than 1 is built from primes — in exactly one way.

visual.alt: Factor tree of 420: 420 splits into 2 and 210, 210 into 2 and 105, 105 into 3 and 35, and 35 into 5 and 7. The leaves are the primes 2, 2, 3, 5 and 7.
visual.caption: $420 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7$

slides.narration: Welcome to Real Numbers, part one. On the screen, the number four hundred and twenty breaks down, branch by branch, until only primes are left. Primes are the atoms of arithmetic. In this lesson you will see that every number has exactly one set of prime atoms, and then use them to find highest common factors and lowest common multiples quickly, even for large numbers.

slides.heading: What you will be able to do
bullets: Break any composite number into primes
State the **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic**
Find **HCF** and **LCM** from prime factorisations
Use $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = $ product — for **two** numbers only
Solve bells, buses, tiles and packing problems
slides.narration: Here are your goals. Notice the warning in the fourth goal: a famous shortcut works for two numbers but fails for three, and examiners love to test that. By the end you will also know how to tell, just from the wording of a word problem, whether it wants the highest common factor or the lowest common multiple.

slides.heading: Primes and composites
slides.body_md: A **prime** has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. A **composite** number has more than two factors. The number 1 is neither.

visual.alt: Table classifying numbers by their factors: 1 has one factor and is neither prime nor composite; 2, 13 and 29 have exactly two factors and are prime; 9 and 21 have more than two factors and are composite.
visual.caption: Count the factors to decide.

slides.narration: Count factors to decide. Two factors exactly, and the number is prime. More than two, and it is composite. The number one has only one factor, so it is neither, and that is why it is never written in a prime factorisation. Also remember that two is the only even prime, because every larger even number has two as an extra factor.

slides.heading: Building a factor tree
slides.body_md: Split off the smallest prime again and again until every branch ends in a prime.

visual.alt: Factor tree of 360 taking out the smallest prime each time: 360 = 2 × 180, 180 = 2 × 90, 90 = 2 × 45, 45 = 3 × 15, 15 = 3 × 5. The leaves are 2, 2, 2, 3, 3 and 5.
visual.caption: $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$

slides.narration: Start with three hundred and sixty. It is even, so take out a two. Keep taking out twos while you can: one hundred and eighty, ninety, forty five. Forty five is odd, so try three: fifteen, then five. Every branch now ends in a prime. Collect them and use powers to write the answer neatly: two cubed, times three squared, times five.

slides.heading: Different trees, same primes
slides.body_md: Start the tree differently and you still end with the same primes.

visual.alt: Two factor trees of 360. Left: 360 = 2 × 180, continuing with 2, 2, 3, 3, 5. Right: 360 = 10 × 36, with 10 = 2 × 5 and 36 = 2 × 18 = 2 × 2 × 9 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Both end with three 2s, two 3s and one 5.
visual.caption: Left: smallest prime first. Right: $360 = 10 \times 36$ first. Same leaves: $2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 5$.

slides.narration: Here is a surprise worth noticing. On the right, someone started with ten times thirty six instead. The tree looks completely different, yet the leaves are the same: three twos, two threes and one five. Try it yourself with any starting split. You will always land on the same primes. That is not luck. It is a theorem.

slides.heading: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
slides.body_md: Every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is **unique**, apart from the order of the factors.
bullets: **Existence:** keep splitting until only primes remain
**Uniqueness:** no number has two different prime factorisations
So $4 \times 630$ is **not** another factorisation of $2520$: $4$ and $630$ are not prime
math: n = p_1^{a_1} \times p_2^{a_2} \times \cdots \times p_k^{a_k}, \quad p_1 < p_2 < \cdots < p_k \text{ primes}
slides.narration: The theorem has two halves. Existence says you can always finish a factor tree. Uniqueness says everyone finishes with the same primes, raised to the same powers. Writing the primes in increasing order gives one standard form. Uniqueness is the powerful half: it lets us say with certainty that a number has no hidden factor of two, or of five.

slides.heading: Quick check: factorise
slides.body_md: Choose the correct prime factorisation.
slides.narration: Divide by two as many times as you can, then try three, then seven. Count how many twos you took out. Then multiply your answer back to check it really gives the number.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: is 7056 a perfect square?
slides.body_md: Use prime factorisation to decide whether $7056$ is a perfect square, and find its square root if it is.
bullets: **Step 2 —** Every exponent ($4, 2, 2$) is even, so $7056$ is a perfect square.
**Step 3 —** Halve each exponent: $\sqrt{7056} = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84$.

visual.alt: Factor tree of 7056: four splits by 2 give 441, then 441 = 3 × 147, 147 = 3 × 49, 49 = 7 × 7. The leaves are four 2s, two 3s and two 7s.
visual.caption: $7056 = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 7^2$

slides.narration: A perfect square is a number times itself, so every prime appears an even number of times. After factorising, just look at the exponents. Four, two and two are all even, so yes. Halving each exponent gives the square root directly, eighty four. This trick also tells you what to multiply by to make a number a perfect square: make every exponent even.

slides.heading: Exponents tell you the shape of a number
slides.body_md: Read squares and cubes straight from the exponents.

visual.alt: Table of four numbers with their prime factorisations: 144 has even exponents so it is a perfect square; 216 has exponents that are multiples of 3 so it is a cube; 729 is 3 to the power 6 so it is both; 1188 needs to be multiplied by 33 to become a perfect square.
visual.caption: Square: all exponents even. Cube: all exponents multiples of 3.

slides.narration: This table turns the idea into a quick test. Square means every exponent is even. Cube means every exponent is a multiple of three. Seven hundred and twenty nine is three to the power six, and six is both even and a multiple of three, so it is both a square and a cube. For eleven eighty eight, the odd exponents tell you exactly which primes are missing.

slides.heading: HCF and LCM from prime factors
slides.body_md: **HCF:** common primes, **smaller** power. **LCM:** every prime, **greater** power.

visual.alt: Two overlapping circles. The left circle, 72, contains the primes 2, 2, 2, 3, 3; the right circle, 120, contains 2, 2, 2, 3, 5. The overlap holds the shared primes 2, 2, 2 and 3. The left-only region holds an extra 3 and the right-only region holds 5.
visual.caption: Overlap $= 2^3 \times 3 = 24 =$ HCF. Everything $= 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360 =$ LCM.

slides.narration: Picture the primes of each number in a circle. The primes they share sit in the overlap, and multiplying them gives the highest common factor, twenty four. Multiplying everything in the picture, overlap counted once, gives the lowest common multiple, three hundred and sixty. In exponent language: smaller power of common primes for the factor, greater power of every prime for the multiple.

slides.heading: The exponent table method
slides.body_md: Write a missing prime as power $0$. Then pick the smaller or the greater power, row by row.

visual.alt: Exponent table for 72 and 120. Prime 2: powers 3 and 3, HCF takes 3, LCM takes 3. Prime 3: powers 2 and 1, HCF takes 1, LCM takes 2. Prime 5: powers 0 and 1, HCF takes 0, LCM takes 1.
visual.caption: HCF $= 2^3 \times 3 = 24$; LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$.

slides.narration: For bigger problems, a table keeps you safe. One row per prime, one column per number. A prime that does not appear gets power zero. For the highest common factor, take the smaller power in each row, so a zero knocks that prime out. For the lowest common multiple, take the greater power. This works for three numbers too: just add a column.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: HCF and LCM of 336 and 180
slides.body_md: Find the HCF and LCM of $336$ and $180$, and check your answer.
bullets: **Step 1 —** $336 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 7$ and $180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5$.
**Step 2 —** Common primes $2, 3$ with smaller powers: HCF $= 2^2 \times 3 = 12$.
**Step 3 —** All primes, greater powers: LCM $= 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 5040$.

visual.alt: Two overlapping circles. 336 has primes 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 7 and 180 has primes 2, 2, 3, 3, 5. The overlap holds 2, 2 and 3. The 336-only region holds 2, 2 and 7; the 180-only region holds 3 and 5.
visual.caption: Overlap: $2^2 \times 3 = 12$. All together: $2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 5040$.

slides.narration: Factorise both numbers first and write the powers clearly. Seven appears only in three thirty six, and five only in one eighty, so neither can be in the highest common factor. Both must be in the lowest common multiple. The final check is quick and worth a mark in your head: the highest common factor times the lowest common multiple should equal the product of the two numbers.

slides.heading: Why HCF × LCM = product, for two numbers
slides.body_md: For each prime, the smaller power plus the greater power equals the sum of both powers.

visual.alt: For 336 and 180, each prime row shows that the smaller exponent plus the greater exponent equals the sum of the two exponents: for 2, 2 plus 4 equals 6; for 3, 1 plus 2 equals 3; for 5 and 7, 0 plus 1 equals 1.
visual.caption: So $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 336 \times 180$, prime by prime.

slides.narration: Why does the shortcut work? Look at any one prime. The factor uses the smaller power, the multiple uses the greater power, and together they use both powers once. That is exactly what the product of the two numbers uses. Every row matches, so the whole products match. Use this to find a missing number: divide the product by the highest common factor.

slides.heading: Quick check: use the product rule
slides.body_md: Two numbers, their product and their HCF are given. Find the LCM.
slides.narration: Which three quantities does the rule connect? Write the rule first, put in the two numbers you know, and then divide. No need to find the original numbers.

slides.heading: Careful: three numbers break the rule
slides.body_md: With three numbers, the **middle** power of each prime is used by neither the HCF nor the LCM.

visual.alt: Table showing the product rule works for the pair 4 and 6, where 24 equals 24, but fails for the triples 4, 6, 10, where 120 is not 240, and 6, 10, 15, where 30 is not 900.
visual.caption: Never use HCF × LCM = product for three or more numbers.

slides.narration: Here is the trap. For four, six and ten, the product of factor and multiple is one hundred and twenty, but the product of the numbers is two hundred and forty. The reason is the middle power. With three numbers, the factor takes the smallest power and the multiple takes the largest, so the middle one is lost. Use the rule for two numbers only.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: three numbers
slides.body_md: Find the HCF and LCM of $48$, $72$ and $108$.
bullets: **Step 2 —** HCF: smallest powers, $2^2 \times 3 = 12$.
**Step 3 —** LCM: greatest powers, $2^4 \times 3^3 = 432$.
**Contrast —** $12 \times 432 = 5184$, but $48 \times 72 \times 108 = 373248$. The product rule does not apply.

visual.alt: Exponent table for 48, 72 and 108: prime 2 has powers 4, 3, 2 so the HCF takes 2 and the LCM takes 4; prime 3 has powers 1, 2, 3 so the HCF takes 1 and the LCM takes 3.
visual.caption: HCF $= 2^2 \times 3 = 12$, LCM $= 2^4 \times 3^3 = 432$.

slides.narration: With three numbers, the exponent table is your best friend. For the factor, take the smallest power in each row. For the multiple, take the largest. Notice the contrast line: the two answers multiplied give about five thousand, while the three numbers multiplied give more than three lakh. So if a question gives you three numbers, find both answers separately.

slides.heading: HCF or LCM? Read the question
slides.body_md: Ask: am I **splitting** quantities into equal pieces, or **waiting** for events to line up?

nodes.label: What does the problem ask for?
Largest size that **divides** all exactly (cut, pack, tile, arrange in rows)
Smallest quantity that all **divide into** (together again, ring together, meet again)
Check: HCF ≤ smallest number ≤ largest number ≤ LCM

visual.alt: Decision chart: if the problem asks for the largest size that divides all the quantities exactly, such as cutting, packing, tiling or arranging, find the HCF; if it asks for the smallest quantity or first time when events coincide, such as bells ringing or buses leaving together, find the LCM. Then check that the HCF is at most the smallest number and the LCM at least the largest.
visual.caption: Size of a piece → HCF. When things happen together again → LCM.

slides.narration: Word problems hide the operation in their wording. If you are cutting, packing, tiling or arranging into equal groups, and want the biggest piece, that is the highest common factor. If you are waiting for bells, lights or buses to coincide again, that is the lowest common multiple. Then sense check: a factor cannot be bigger than the numbers, and a multiple cannot be smaller.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: buses leaving together
slides.body_md: From Majestic bus station in Bengaluru, buses on three routes leave every $18$, $24$ and $30$ minutes. All three leave at 6:00 a.m. When do they next leave together?
bullets: **Step 1 —** "Next together" → LCM.
**Step 3 —** LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$ minutes $= 6$ hours.

visual.alt: Departure times of three bus routes plotted as dots on three rows: route 1 every 18 minutes, route 2 every 24 minutes, route 3 every 30 minutes. The first time after the start when all three rows have a dot at the same minute is 360 minutes, which is 12 noon.
visual.caption: Departures line up again at the least common multiple, 360 minutes.

slides.narration: Look at the dot chart. Each row is one route, and each dot is a departure. The rows have dots at different rhythms, and the first time all three rows have a dot in the same column is three hundred and sixty minutes. That is six hours, so twelve noon. Always convert your answer back into a clock time if the question gives one.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: cutting ribbons
slides.body_md: A tailor in Surat has ribbons $252$ cm and $336$ cm long. She cuts both into pieces of equal length, as long as possible, with nothing left over. Find the piece length and the number of pieces.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Equal pieces with nothing left → the length divides both → HCF.
**Step 2 —** $252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7$, $336 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 7$.
**Step 3 —** HCF $= 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84$ cm.

visual.alt: Table: the 252 centimetre ribbon gives 3 pieces of 84 centimetres and the 336 centimetre ribbon gives 4 pieces, 7 pieces in all.
visual.caption: The longest common piece is the HCF, 84 cm.

slides.narration: Here we are cutting, so we want the biggest length that divides both ribbons exactly: the highest common factor, eighty four centimetres. Many students stop there, but the question also asks for the number of pieces. Divide each ribbon by eighty four and add. Always reread the question at the end to make sure you have answered every part.

slides.heading: Quick check: traffic signals
slides.body_md: Three signals turn green at different intervals. When are they green together again?
slides.narration: Is this a cutting problem or a waiting problem? Decide that first, then factorise the three intervals and choose your powers.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Every composite number is a product of primes in exactly **one** way (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic)
HCF: **common** primes, **smaller** powers. LCM: **all** primes, **greater** powers
$\text{HCF}(a, b) \times \text{LCM}(a, b) = ab$ — two numbers only
Perfect square: all exponents even; cube: multiples of $3$
Splitting into equal pieces → HCF; events coinciding → LCM

visual.alt: Summary table for 72 and 120: factorise into 2 cubed times 3 squared and 2 cubed times 3 times 5; the HCF is 24, the LCM is 360, and 24 times 360 equals 8640, which is 72 times 120.
visual.caption: One worked pair that shows every rule.

slides.narration: Let us pull it together. Factorise first, always. Then the highest common factor takes common primes with smaller powers, and the lowest common multiple takes every prime with greater powers. The product check works for two numbers only. And in word problems, ask whether you are splitting things into equal pieces or waiting for things to happen together.

slides.heading: Exam tips: how marks are awarded
bullets: **2-mark HCF/LCM:** factorisations 1 + HCF and LCM 1. Show the prime factorisations — answers alone may lose marks
**Word problems (3–5 marks):** identify HCF or LCM 1, factorisations 1, value 1, final answer in the units asked (time, pieces, rupees) 1
**Mistake:** taking the greater power for HCF (that is the LCM)
**Mistake:** using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers
**Mistake:** stopping at the HCF when the question asks for the number of pieces, boxes or rows
**Mistake:** writing $1$ or a composite number (like $4$) in a prime factorisation
slides.narration: In the board exam, the method earns marks, so always show the prime factorisations, not just the final number. In word problems, one mark usually goes to saying clearly whether you need the factor or the multiple. The most common slips are swapping smaller and greater powers, using the product rule for three numbers, and stopping one step early. Finish with units or a clock time.

decks.title: Real Numbers — Part 2: Irrational numbers and proofs
goals: Distinguish rational and irrational numbers with examples
Use the fact that if a prime divides a², it divides a
Prove by contradiction that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational
Prove that numbers such as 4 − 3√2 are irrational
Decide whether sums and products involving surds are rational

slides.heading: Real Numbers, Part 2: Irrational numbers
slides.body_md: $\sqrt2$ is a real point on the number line — but no fraction lands exactly on it.

visual.alt: A number line marked minus 1, 0, 1, 2 and 3. A right triangle with legs of 1 unit stands on the segment from 0 to 1, with a vertical leg at 1. Its hypotenuse from 0 has length root 2; a circle centred at 0 through the top of the triangle cuts the number line at root 2, between 1 and 2.
visual.caption: The circle swings the hypotenuse onto the line: $\sqrt2 \approx 1.414$.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. Draw a right triangle with both short sides one unit long. Its long side is the square root of two. Swing that length down onto the number line with a compass, and it lands between one and two. So the square root of two is a genuine point on the line. In this lesson we prove that no fraction, however clever, ever lands exactly on it.

slides.heading: Rational and irrational numbers
slides.body_md: A number is **rational** if it can be written as $\dfrac pq$ with $p, q$ integers and $q \ne 0$. A real number that cannot be written this way is **irrational**.

visual.alt: Table: minus 7, 0.75 and the square root of 49 are rational because each can be written as a fraction; root 2, root 3, root 5 and pi are irrational.
visual.caption: Rationals and irrationals together make up the real numbers.

slides.narration: Rational means you can write the number as one integer over another, with a non-zero bottom. Whole numbers, negatives and simple decimals all qualify. Be careful with roots: the square root of forty nine is just seven, which is rational. But the square roots of two, three and five are not. And pi is irrational: twenty two over seven is only a handy approximation.

slides.heading: Where does √2 come from?
slides.body_md: A square tile of side $1$ m has a diagonal of $\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2$ m.

visual.alt: A square ABCD with sides 1 metre. The diagonal AC is dashed and labelled root 2 metres; triangle ABC, with a right angle at B, is shaded.
visual.caption: The diagonal of a unit square is $\sqrt2$ — a length you can draw but not write as a fraction.

slides.narration: Irrational numbers are not exotic. Take a one metre square floor tile in your classroom. By Pythagoras, its diagonal is the square root of two metres. You can measure it, about one point four one four metres, but the digits never settle into a fraction. The Greeks were so shocked by this discovery that, legend says, they tried to keep it secret.

slides.heading: The key fact: a prime that divides a² divides a
slides.body_md: Let $p$ be a prime and $a$ a positive integer. If $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$.
bullets: **Why:** if $a = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_n$ (primes), then $a^2 = p_1 p_1 p_2 p_2 \cdots p_n p_n$
By uniqueness, the only primes in $a^2$ are the primes of $a$
So a prime $p$ dividing $a^2$ is one of $p_1, \dots, p_n$, and divides $a$

visual.alt: Table of examples: 3 divides 36 and also 6; 5 divides 100 and also 10; but 4, which is not prime, divides 36 without dividing 6.
visual.caption: The fact needs $p$ to be prime.

slides.narration: This fact is the engine of every proof in this lesson. It comes straight from the Fundamental Theorem: squaring a number only doubles its primes, it never creates new ones. So if a prime divides a squared, it was already in a. Look at the last row of the table. Four divides thirty six but not six, because four is not prime. The word prime is essential.

slides.heading: Proof by contradiction: the plan
slides.body_md: We cannot test every fraction, so we show that **assuming** a fraction exists leads to nonsense.

nodes.label: Assume the **opposite** of what you want

visual.alt: Flow chart of proof by contradiction: assume the opposite of the statement, reason correctly step by step, reach an impossible conclusion, and conclude that the assumption was false.
visual.caption: To prove "$\sqrt3$ is irrational", assume "$\sqrt3$ is rational".

slides.narration: There are infinitely many fractions, so we cannot check them all. Instead we use a detective trick. Pretend the square root of three is a fraction, and follow the logic carefully. If every step is correct but we end up with something impossible, the only thing that can be wrong is our starting assumption. That is proof by contradiction.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: √3 is irrational (setting up)
slides.body_md: **To prove:** $\sqrt3$ is irrational.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Suppose $\sqrt3$ is rational: $\sqrt3 = \dfrac ab$, where $a, b$ are integers, $b \ne 0$, and $a, b$ are **co-prime** (fraction in lowest terms).
**Step 2 —** Square both sides: $3 = \dfrac{a^2}{b^2}$, so $3b^2 = a^2$ … (1)
**Step 3 —** So $3$ divides $a^2$. As $3$ is prime, $3$ divides $a$. Write $a = 3c$ … (2)
slides.narration: Why insist on co-prime? Any fraction can be reduced to lowest terms, so this costs us nothing, and it is exactly what we will contradict. Squaring removes the root and gives three b squared equals a squared. Now the key fact kicks in: three is prime and divides a squared, so three divides a. We record a equals three c for the next step.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: √3 is irrational (the contradiction)
bullets: **Step 5 —** So $3$ divides $b^2$, and therefore $3$ divides $b$.
**Step 6 —** Now $3$ divides **both** $a$ and $b$. This contradicts that $a$ and $b$ are co-prime.
**Conclusion —** The assumption is false, so $\sqrt3$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$

visual.alt: Proof chain for the square root of 3: assume it equals a over b in lowest terms, square to get 3 b squared equals a squared, deduce 3 divides a, substitute a equals 3 c, deduce 3 divides b, reach a contradiction with lowest terms, conclude irrational.
visual.caption: Every irrationality proof in this chapter follows this chain.

slides.narration: Substitute and simplify: b squared equals three c squared. Now the same key fact works on b. So three divides a and three divides b. But we chose a and b with no common factor. That is the contradiction, and the proof is complete. Exactly the same chain proves the square roots of two and five are irrational. Only the prime changes.

slides.heading: Quick check: the starting assumption
slides.body_md: What exactly do we assume at the start of the proof?
slides.narration: Think about which property of a and b the contradiction attacks at the very end. That property must be part of the assumption.

slides.heading: Rational and irrational: what combinations give
slides.body_md: If $r$ is rational and $x$ irrational: $r + x$ and (for $r \ne 0$) $rx$ are irrational.

visual.alt: Table of combinations: a rational plus an irrational is always irrational, as is a non-zero rational times an irrational; but the sum or product of two irrationals can be rational, for example root 3 plus minus root 3 is 0 and root 2 times root 8 is 4.
visual.caption: Only the first two rows are safe rules.

slides.narration: Here are the rules you may use. Rational plus irrational is always irrational. A non-zero rational times an irrational is always irrational. Both follow from a tiny contradiction argument. But two irrationals together can give anything. The square root of two times the square root of eight is four. So never claim that two irrationals always give an irrational.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: prove 4 − 3√2 is irrational
slides.body_md: Given that $\sqrt2$ is irrational, prove that $4 - 3\sqrt2$ is irrational.
bullets: **Step 1 —** Suppose $4 - 3\sqrt2 = r$, where $r$ is rational.
**Step 2 —** Then $3\sqrt2 = 4 - r$, so $\sqrt2 = \dfrac{4 - r}{3}$.
**Step 3 —** $4 - r$ is rational, and dividing by $3$ keeps it rational, so $\sqrt2$ would be rational.
**Step 4 —** This contradicts the given fact. Hence $4 - 3\sqrt2$ is irrational. $\blacksquare$

visual.alt: Flow of the proof: assume 4 minus 3 root 2 equals a rational r, isolate root 2 as 4 minus r over 3, note the right side is rational, which contradicts root 2 being irrational.
visual.caption: Isolate the root using only operations that keep rationals rational.

slides.narration: This is a very common three mark question. The strategy is always the same: assume the whole expression is a rational number r, then isolate the root using only subtraction and division by a non-zero number. Those operations keep rational numbers rational, so the root itself would be rational. That contradicts what we already know. State the contradiction clearly; it carries a mark.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: when the rules do not apply
slides.body_md: Decide whether each number is rational or irrational: (i) $\sqrt2 \times \sqrt{18}$ (ii) $(\sqrt5 + 1)^2$ (iii) $\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{\sqrt3}$.
bullets: **(i)** $\sqrt{36} = 6$: **rational**, though both factors are irrational.
**(ii)** $5 + 2\sqrt5 + 1 = 6 + 2\sqrt5$: rational $+$ irrational, so **irrational**.
**(iii)** $\sqrt{\dfrac{12}{3}} = \sqrt4 = 2$: **rational**.
**Lesson —** Simplify first; decide afterwards.

visual.alt: Table: root 2 times root 18 simplifies to 6, rational; root 5 plus 1, squared, simplifies to 6 plus 2 root 5, irrational; root 12 over root 3 simplifies to 2, rational.
visual.caption: Simplify before you classify.

slides.narration: An expression full of roots can still be rational, so never judge by appearance. Simplify first. In the first case the roots multiply to the square root of thirty six, which is six. In the second, expanding the square leaves a two root five term that does not cancel, so the result is irrational. In the third, dividing roots gives the square root of four.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the irrational
slides.body_md: Only one of these numbers is irrational. Simplify each one first.
slides.narration: Look for perfect squares hiding inside each root. If a root simplifies to a whole number, the number is rational.

slides.heading: Common traps
slides.body_md: Know these before the exam.

rows: roots do not add like that

visual.alt: Table of five statements: root 4 is irrational is false because it equals 2; pi equals 22 over 7 is false; if 4 divides a squared then 4 divides a is false, for example a equals 6; root 2 plus root 3 equals root 5 is false; 5 root 7 is irrational is true.
visual.caption: Each false statement here appears in students' answers every year.

slides.narration: These five lines collect the mistakes examiners see most. The square root of a perfect square is rational. Pi is not twenty two over seven. The key divisibility fact needs a prime. Roots do not add under the root sign: the square root of two plus the square root of three is about three point one five, not two point two four. And a rational multiple of an irrational stays irrational.

slides.heading: Quick check: assertion and reason
slides.body_md: Decide whether the assertion and the reason are true, and whether the reason explains the assertion.
slides.narration: Work out the product first. Then ask whether the reason is always true. One example can be enough to show that an always statement is false.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Rational: $\dfrac pq$ with $q \ne 0$. Irrational: cannot be written so ($\sqrt2, \sqrt3, \sqrt5, \pi$)
If a prime $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$ (from uniqueness of factorisation)
Proof for $\sqrt p$: assume $\dfrac ab$ in lowest terms → $p \mid a$ → $p \mid b$ → contradiction
rational $+$ irrational, and non-zero rational $\times$ irrational, are irrational
Two irrationals can combine to a rational: simplify first

slides.narration: Here is the whole lesson in one chain, shown for the square root of five. Assume a fraction in lowest terms, square, use the prime fact twice, and reach a common factor that should not exist. For expressions like four minus three root two, assume rational and isolate the root. And remember that only the first two combination rules are guaranteed.

**Prove $r + s\sqrt p$ irrational (2–3 marks):** assume rational 1, isolate the root 1, contradiction 1

sections.heading: 1. Primes, composites and factor trees
sections.body_md:
A **prime** number has exactly two factors, $1$ and itself: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, \dots$ A **composite** number has more than two factors. The number $1$ is neither prime nor composite, and $2$ is the only even prime.

To **factorise** a composite number, split off primes repeatedly — by a factor tree or by repeated division — until only primes remain. Write the result with powers in increasing order of primes, e.g. $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$.

**Divisibility shortcuts** help: $2$ (last digit even), $3$ (digit sum divisible by 3), $5$ (last digit 0 or 5), $11$ (alternating digit sum divisible by 11).

key_terms.definition_md: A natural number with exactly two factors, $1$ and itself.
A natural number greater than $1$ with more than two factors.
Writing a number as a product of primes, e.g. $84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$.

visual.caption: Factor tree of $360$.

sections.heading: 2. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
sections.body_md:
**Theorem.** Every composite number can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is **unique**, apart from the order in which the primes occur.

Consequences you will use:

- A number ends in $0$ exactly when it is divisible by $10 = 2 \times 5$, so its factorisation must contain both $2$ and $5$. Hence $12^n = 2^{2n} \times 3^n$ never ends in $0$.
- **Perfect square:** every exponent even. **Perfect cube:** every exponent a multiple of $3$. To make $1188 = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 11$ a square, multiply by $3 \times 11 = 33$.
- "Factorisations" such as $2520 = 4 \times 630$ are not prime factorisations; reduce every factor to primes.

*Not in the 2026–27 syllabus:* Euclid's division lemma and algorithm, and decimal expansions of rational numbers.

key_terms.definition_md: Every composite number is a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from order.
Numbers whose HCF is $1$, e.g. $8$ and $15$.

sections.heading: 3. HCF and LCM by prime factorisation
sections.body_md:
- **HCF** (highest common factor) $=$ product of the **common** primes, each with its **smaller** power.
- **LCM** (lowest common multiple) $=$ product of **all** primes that occur, each with its **greater** power.

Working: $336 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 7$ and $180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5$, so $\text{HCF} = 2^2 \times 3 = 12$ and $\text{LCM} = 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 5040$.

For **three numbers**, use primes common to **all three** for the HCF: $\text{HCF}(48, 72, 108) = 2^2 \times 3 = 12$, $\text{LCM} = 2^4 \times 3^3 = 432$.

An exponent table (one row per prime, power $0$ when a prime is missing) prevents slips.

key_terms.definition_md: The largest number that divides each of the given numbers exactly.
The smallest number that is a multiple of each of the given numbers.

formulas.label: m, n = powers of p in the two numbers

visual.caption: HCF $=$ overlap $= 12$; LCM $=$ everything $= 5040$.

sections.heading: 4. HCF × LCM = product (two numbers only)
sections.body_md:
For any two natural numbers $a$ and $b$, $\text{HCF}(a, b) \times \text{LCM}(a, b) = a \times b$, because for each prime $\min(m, n) + \max(m, n) = m + n$.

Use it to find a missing number: if $\text{HCF} = 23$, $\text{LCM} = 1449$ and one number is $161$, the other is $\dfrac{23 \times 1449}{161} = 207$.

**It fails for three numbers:** for $4, 6, 10$, $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 2 \times 60 = 120$, but $4 \times 6 \times 10 = 240$.

Useful facts: the HCF always divides the LCM; co-prime numbers have $\text{HCF} = 1$ and $\text{LCM} = $ product; consecutive numbers are co-prime.

key_terms.definition_md: $\text{HCF}(a, b) \times \text{LCM}(a, b) = ab$ for two numbers.

visual.alt: Table showing HCF times LCM equals the product for 4 and 6 (24 and 24) but not for 4, 6, 10 (120 against 240) or 6, 10, 15 (30 against 900).
visual.caption: The rule holds for pairs only.

sections.heading: 5. Word problems on HCF and LCM
sections.body_md:
**HCF problems** ask for the **largest** size that divides several quantities exactly: cutting ribbons or rods, packing sweets, tiling floors with square tiles, arranging groups in equal rows, spacing poles.

**LCM problems** ask for the **smallest** quantity or the **first time** at which events coincide: bells ringing together, buses or trains leaving together, runners meeting at the start, lights blinking together.

**Remainder variants:** "largest number dividing 245 and 1029 leaving remainders 5 and 9" → HCF of $240$ and $1020$ $= 60$. "Smallest number leaving remainder 5 when divided by 12, 16, 24, 36" → LCM $+ 5$.

Always finish with what is asked: the number of pieces, a clock time, or a cost.

key_terms.definition_md: A number that each given number divides exactly; the LCM is the smallest.

sections.heading: 6. Rational and irrational numbers
sections.body_md:
A number is **rational** if it can be written as $\dfrac pq$, where $p$ and $q$ are integers and $q \ne 0$. A real number that is not rational is **irrational**. Examples of irrationals: $\sqrt2, \sqrt3, \sqrt5, \sqrt6, \pi$. The square root of a natural number that is not a perfect square is irrational; $\sqrt{49} = 7$ is rational.

Irrational numbers are real lengths: the diagonal of a $1$ m square tile is $\sqrt2$ m, and $\sqrt2$ can be marked on the number line with a compass.

$\pi$ is irrational; $\dfrac{22}{7}$ and $3.14$ are only approximations.

key_terms.definition_md: A number of the form $\dfrac pq$, $p, q$ integers, $q \ne 0$.
A real number that cannot be written as $\dfrac pq$.

sections.heading: 7. Proving that √2, √3 and √5 are irrational
sections.body_md:
**Key fact.** If a prime $p$ divides $a^2$, then $p$ divides $a$. (By uniqueness of factorisation, $a^2$ has the same primes as $a$.) It is false for non-primes: $4$ divides $36$ but not $6$.

**Proof that $\sqrt5$ is irrational.** Suppose $\sqrt5 = \dfrac ab$ with $a, b$ co-prime and $b \ne 0$. Then $5b^2 = a^2$, so $5 \mid a^2$ and hence $5 \mid a$; write $a = 5c$. Then $5b^2 = 25c^2$, i.e. $b^2 = 5c^2$, so $5 \mid b^2$ and $5 \mid b$. Thus $5$ divides both $a$ and $b$, contradicting co-primality. So $\sqrt5$ is irrational.

The same steps with $2$ or $3$ prove $\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt3$ irrational.

key_terms.definition_md: Assume the opposite of the statement, reason correctly to an impossibility, and conclude the assumption was false.

sections.heading: 8. Sums and products with irrational numbers
sections.body_md:
If $r$ is rational and $x$ is irrational:

- $r + x$ and $r - x$ are irrational;
- $rx$ and $\dfrac xr$ are irrational when $r \ne 0$.

**Method for "prove $4 - 3\sqrt2$ is irrational":** suppose it equals a rational $r$; then $\sqrt2 = \dfrac{4 - r}{3}$ would be rational, a contradiction.

Two irrationals can give a rational: $\sqrt2 \times \sqrt{18} = 6$, $(3 + \sqrt2) + (3 - \sqrt2) = 6$, $(3 + \sqrt2)(3 - \sqrt2) = 7$. Simplify before classifying.

key_terms.definition_md: An irrational root such as $\sqrt2$ or $3\sqrt5$.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are awarded**
- *HCF/LCM (2–3 marks):* prime factorisations 1, HCF and LCM 1, verification or final answer 1. Answers without factorisations can lose the method mark.
- *Word problems (3–5 marks):* identifying HCF or LCM 1, factorisations 1, value 1, answer in the asked form (pieces, clock time, cost) 1–2.
- *Irrationality proofs (3 marks):* assumption with co-prime $a, b$ ½, $p \mid a$ with "p is prime" 1, $p \mid b$ 1, contradiction and conclusion ½.
- *Prove $r + s\sqrt p$ irrational (2–3 marks):* assume rational, isolate the root, state the contradiction.

**Common mistakes**
1. Taking greater powers for the HCF (that gives the LCM).
2. Using HCF × LCM = product for three numbers.
3. Writing $1$ or composite numbers in a prime factorisation.
4. Stopping at the HCF when the number of pieces or boxes is asked.
5. Forgetting "co-prime" in the assumption of an irrationality proof.
6. Using "$p \mid a^2 \Rightarrow p \mid a$" for a non-prime $p$.
7. Claiming the sum or product of two irrationals is always irrational.
8. Treating $\pi$ as $\dfrac{22}{7}$.

questions.stem_md: The prime factorisation of $1176$ is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Divide by the smallest primes: $1176 \div 2 = 588$, $588 \div 2 = 294$, $294 \div 2 = 147$, $147 \div 3 = 49$, $49 \div 7 = 7$.

**Step 2.** So $1176 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7^2$. **Check:** $8 \times 3 \times 49 = 1176$.

Option (b) is $588$ (one factor 2 missing), (c) is $504$ and (d) is $2352$.

questions.stem_md: For a natural number $n$, which of these numbers ends with the digit $0$ for **every** value of $n$?
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** A number ends with $0$ exactly when it is divisible by $10 = 2 \times 5$, so its prime factorisation must contain both $2$ and $5$.

**Step 2.** $20^n = 2^{2n} \times 5^n$ contains both, so it always ends with $0$.

**Step 3.** $6^n = 2^n \times 3^n$ has no $5$; $15^n = 3^n \times 5^n$ has no $2$; $21^n = 3^n \times 7^n$ has neither. By the uniqueness of prime factorisation, no other factor can appear, so none of these can ever end with $0$.

questions.stem_md: How many **distinct** prime factors does $2310$ have?
questions.solution_md: $2310 = 2 \times 1155 = 2 \times 3 \times 385 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 77 = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11$. There are $5$ distinct primes: $2, 3, 5, 7, 11$.

questions.stem_md: The HCF of $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ and $2^2 \times 3^3 \times 7$ is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** The common primes are $2$ and $3$ ($5$ and $7$ are not common).

**Step 2.** Take the **smaller** power of each: $2^2$ and $3^2$. HCF $= 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$.

Option (c) $7560 = 2^3 \times 3^3 \times 5 \times 7$ is the LCM (greater powers of every prime). Option (a) takes $2^3$, the greater power of $2$.

questions.stem_md: Two natural numbers have HCF $12$, and their product is $2160$. Their LCM is
questions.solution_md:
For two numbers, $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = $ product of the numbers. So $\text{LCM} = \dfrac{2160}{12} = 180$.

Option (b) subtracts instead of dividing; option (c) multiplies $2160 \times 12$.

questions.stem_md: The HCF of any two consecutive natural numbers $n$ and $n + 1$ is
questions.solution_md: Any common factor of $n$ and $n + 1$ also divides their difference $(n + 1) - n = 1$. The only natural number dividing $1$ is $1$, so the HCF is $1$: consecutive numbers are always **co-prime**. For example, HCF$(14, 15) = 1$.

questions.stem_md: The LCM of $12$, $18$ and $30$ is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $12 = 2^2 \times 3$, $18 = 2 \times 3^2$, $30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5$.

**Step 2.** LCM takes the greatest power of every prime that appears: $2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180$.

Option (d) is the HCF, option (b) is the product $12 \times 18 \times 30$, and (a) is a common multiple but not the least.

questions.stem_md: Which pair **cannot** be the HCF and LCM (in that order) of two natural numbers?
questions.solution_md:
The HCF divides each number, and each number divides the LCM, so the **HCF must divide the LCM**.

$72 \div 6 = 12$, $125 \div 5 = 25$ and $63 \div 9 = 7$ are whole numbers, but $90 \div 12 = 7.5$ is not. So $12$ and $90$ cannot be an HCF–LCM pair.

questions.stem_md: Three traffic signals on a road in Chandigarh turn green every $48$ seconds, $72$ seconds and $108$ seconds. They all turn green together at 7:00 a.m. After how many seconds will they next turn green together?
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** "Next together" asks for the **least common multiple**.

**Step 2.** $48 = 2^4 \times 3$, $72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$, $108 = 2^2 \times 3^3$.

**Step 3.** LCM $= 2^4 \times 3^3 = 432$ s, that is $7$ minutes $12$ seconds after 7:00 a.m.

Option (b) is the HCF. Option (c) $216$ is not a multiple of $48$, and (d) is a common multiple but not the least.

questions.stem_md: When $172$ notebooks and $259$ pens are shared equally among the students of a class, $4$ notebooks and $7$ pens are left over. The greatest possible number of students in the class is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** The students received $172 - 4 = 168$ notebooks and $259 - 7 = 252$ pens, so the number of students divides both $168$ and $252$ exactly.

**Step 2.** $168 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7$ and $252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7$, so HCF $= 2^2 \times 3 \times 7 = 84$.

**Check:** $172 = 2 \times 84 + 4$ and $259 = 3 \times 84 + 7$. Options (c) and (a) also leave these remainders but are not the greatest; $168$ does not divide $252$.

questions.stem_md: Which of these numbers is **irrational**?
questions.solution_md:
$\sqrt{196} = 14$; $\dfrac{\sqrt{12}}{\sqrt{3}} = \sqrt{4} = 2$; $(\sqrt5)^2 = 5$ — all rational.

$\sqrt{18} = \sqrt{9 \times 2} = 3\sqrt{2}$, a non-zero rational times the irrational $\sqrt2$, so it is irrational.

questions.stem_md: The product $\sqrt{5} \times \sqrt{20}$ is
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt5 \times \sqrt{20} = \sqrt{100} = 10$, which is rational. This shows that the product of two irrational numbers **can** be rational. Option (a) forgets the square root.

questions.stem_md: To prove by contradiction that $\sqrt{5}$ is irrational, we begin by assuming $\sqrt{5} = \dfrac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are
questions.solution_md: We assume the opposite of what we want to prove: $\sqrt5$ is rational. Any rational number can be written in lowest terms, so $a$ and $b$ are integers with **no common factor other than 1** (co-prime) and $b \ne 0$. The contradiction later is that $5$ divides both $a$ and $b$.

questions.stem_md: Let $p$ be a prime and $a$ a positive integer. If $p$ divides $a^2$, then
questions.solution_md:
By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic, the primes in $a^2$ are exactly the primes in $a$ (each appearing twice as often). So if $p$ divides $a^2$, $p$ is one of the primes of $a$, and $p$ divides $a$.

Option (d) fails: $p = 2$ divides $6^2 = 36$, but $4$ does not divide $6$.

questions.stem_md: The number $(2 + \sqrt{3})(2 - \sqrt{3})$ is
questions.solution_md: Use $(x + y)(x - y) = x^2 - y^2$: $(2 + \sqrt3)(2 - \sqrt3) = 4 - 3 = 1$, which is rational. Option (d) adds $4 + 3$ instead of subtracting.

questions.stem_md: If $x$ is a rational number and $y$ is an irrational number, then $x + y$ is
questions.solution_md: Suppose $x + y = q$ were rational. Then $y = q - x$ would be a difference of two rationals, which is rational — a contradiction. So $x + y$ is always irrational. (Contrast: the sum of **two irrationals** can be rational, e.g. $\sqrt2 + (-\sqrt2) = 0$.)

questions.stem_md: The smallest natural number $k$ for which $2^4 \times 3^2 \times k$ is a perfect cube is
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** In a perfect cube every prime exponent is a multiple of $3$.

**Step 2.** $2^4$ needs two more $2$s to become $2^6$; $3^2$ needs one more $3$ to become $3^3$.

**Step 3.** $k = 2^2 \times 3 = 12$. **Check:** $2^4 \times 3^2 \times 12 = 2^6 \times 3^3 = 1728 = 12^3$.

Option (b) $6$ gives $2^5 \times 3^3$, not a cube.

questions.stem_md: For the numbers $6$, $10$ and $15$, which statement is true?
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $6 = 2 \times 3$, $10 = 2 \times 5$, $15 = 3 \times 5$. No prime is common to all three, so HCF $= 1$.

**Step 2.** LCM $= 2 \times 3 \times 5 = 30$, so $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 30$, while $6 \times 10 \times 15 = 900$.

The rule "HCF × LCM = product" holds for **two** numbers only. Option (c) wrongly takes a factor common to just two of the numbers.

questions.solution_md: R is true: for each prime, $\min(m, n) + \max(m, n) = m + n$. A is false. For $4$, $6$, $10$: HCF $= 2$, LCM $= 60$, so $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 120$, but $4 \times 6 \times 10 = 240$.

**Assertion (A):** If $p$ and $q$ are two different prime numbers, then $\text{LCM}(p, q) = pq$.

**Reason (R):** If $p$ and $q$ are two different prime numbers, then $\text{HCF}(p, q) = p$.

questions.solution_md: Two different primes have no common factor except $1$, so $\text{HCF}(p, q) = 1$ (R is false) and $\text{LCM}(p, q) = \dfrac{pq}{1} = pq$ (A is true). For example, $\text{LCM}(5, 7) = 35$.

questions.stem_md: Every natural number greater than 1 is either a prime or can be written as a product of primes.
questions.solution_md: This is the existence half of the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Keep dividing a composite number by primes until only primes are left, as in a factor tree.

questions.stem_md: Two different natural numbers can have exactly the same prime factorisation.
questions.solution_md: If two numbers had the same primes with the same powers, multiplying them out would give the same number. The factorisation is unique to each number, so different numbers have different factorisations.

questions.stem_md: If $\text{HCF}(a, b) = a$, then $\text{LCM}(a, b) = b$.
questions.solution_md: $\text{HCF}(a, b) = a$ means $a$ divides $b$. Then $b$ is a common multiple and no smaller multiple of $b$ exists, so $\text{LCM}(a, b) = b$. Also $\dfrac{ab}{a} = b$. Example: $\text{HCF}(8, 24) = 8$, $\text{LCM}(8, 24) = 24$.

questions.stem_md: $\pi$ is a rational number because $\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}$.
questions.solution_md: $\pi$ is irrational. $\dfrac{22}{7}$ is only a convenient approximation: $\dfrac{22}{7} \approx 3.1429$, while $\pi \approx 3.1416$.

questions.stem_md: The sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational.
questions.solution_md: Counter-example: $\sqrt3$ and $-\sqrt3$ are both irrational, but $\sqrt3 + (-\sqrt3) = 0$, which is rational. Another: $(5 + \sqrt2) + (5 - \sqrt2) = 10$.

questions.stem_md: $945 = 3^3 \times 5 \times$ ___
questions.solution_md: $3^3 \times 5 = 135$ and $945 \div 135 = 7$, which is prime. So $945 = 3^3 \times 5 \times 7$.

questions.stem_md: Given $\text{HCF}(144, 234) = 18$, the value of $\text{LCM}(144, 234)$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: $\text{LCM} = \dfrac{144 \times 234}{18} = 8 \times 234 = 1872$.

questions.stem_md: The smallest natural number divisible by each of $8$, $9$ and $10$ is ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the LCM: $8 = 2^3$, $9 = 3^2$, $10 = 2 \times 5$, so LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$.

questions.stem_md: In the proof that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational, squaring $\sqrt{3} = \dfrac{a}{b}$ gives $a^2 =$ ___ $\times\, b^2$.
questions.solution_md: $\sqrt3 = \dfrac ab \Rightarrow 3 = \dfrac{a^2}{b^2} \Rightarrow a^2 = 3b^2$. So $3$ divides $a^2$, hence $3$ divides $a$.

questions.stem_md: The only even prime number is ___.
questions.solution_md: Every even number is divisible by $2$; any even number greater than $2$ therefore has the factor $2$ besides $1$ and itself, so it is composite. Only $2$ is an even prime.

questions.stem_md: Using prime factorisation, find the HCF of $405$ and $2520$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $405 = 3^4 \times 5$ and $2520 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$.

**Step 2.** Common primes with smaller powers: $3^2$ and $5$.

**Step 3.** HCF $= 3^2 \times 5 = 45$.

questions.stem_md: Using prime factorisation, find the LCM of $405$ and $2520$.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $405 = 3^4 \times 5$ and $2520 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$.

**Step 2.** Every prime with its greater power: $2^3$, $3^4$, $5$, $7$.

**Step 3.** LCM $= 8 \times 81 \times 5 \times 7 = 22680$.

**Check:** HCF $= 45$ and $45 \times 22680 = 1020600 = 405 \times 2520$.

marking_scheme.step: Greatest powers of all primes chosen

questions.stem_md: The product of two natural numbers is $6480$ and their HCF is $12$. Find their LCM.
questions.solution_md: $\text{LCM} = \dfrac{\text{product}}{\text{HCF}} = \dfrac{6480}{12} = 540$.

questions.stem_md: For Diwali, Raghav has $84$ laddoos and $126$ barfis. He packs them in boxes so that every box holds the same number of sweets and only one kind of sweet, using as few boxes as possible. How many boxes does he need?
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Fewest boxes means the **largest** number per box that divides both $84$ and $126$: the HCF.

**Step 2.** $84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$, $126 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 7$, so HCF $= 2 \times 3 \times 7 = 42$ sweets per box.

**Step 3.** Boxes $= \dfrac{84}{42} + \dfrac{126}{42} = 2 + 3 = 5$.

questions.stem_md: Three strings of Diwali lights blink every $15$ s, $20$ s and $25$ s. They blink together at the moment they are switched on. How many more times do they blink together in the next one hour?
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** They blink together every $\text{LCM}(15, 20, 25)$ seconds. $15 = 3 \times 5$, $20 = 2^2 \times 5$, $25 = 5^2$, so LCM $= 2^2 \times 3 \times 5^2 = 300$ s.

**Step 2.** One hour $= 3600$ s, and $\dfrac{3600}{300} = 12$. They blink together $12$ more times (the last one exactly at the end of the hour).

questions.stem_md: A rectangular verandah measures $5.04$ m by $3.36$ m. It is to be paved with identical square tiles, with no tile cut. What is the side of the **largest** such tile, in centimetres?
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** Work in centimetres: $504$ cm and $336$ cm. The tile side must divide both, and be as large as possible: the HCF.

**Step 2.** $504 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 7$ and $336 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 7$, so HCF $= 2^3 \times 3 \times 7 = 168$ cm.

**Check:** $504 \div 168 = 3$ and $336 \div 168 = 2$, so $3 \times 2 = 6$ tiles fit exactly.

marking_scheme.step: Converts to cm and identifies HCF

questions.stem_md: Two numbers have HCF $2^2 \times 3$ and LCM $2^4 \times 3^3 \times 5$. One of the numbers is $240$. Find the other number.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** HCF $= 12$, LCM $= 16 \times 27 \times 5 = 2160$.

**Step 2.** Other number $= \dfrac{\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM}}{240} = \dfrac{12 \times 2160}{240} = 108$.

**Check:** $108 = 2^2 \times 3^3$ and $240 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 5$ give HCF $2^2 \times 3$ and LCM $2^4 \times 3^3 \times 5$. ✓

marking_scheme.step: Uses HCF × LCM = product with HCF = 12, LCM = 2160

questions.stem_md: Find the smallest natural number by which $1188$ must be multiplied so that the product is a perfect square.
questions.solution_md:
**Step 1.** $1188 = 2^2 \times 3^3 \times 11$.

**Step 2.** In a perfect square every exponent is even. $2^2$ is fine; $3^3$ needs one more $3$; $11$ needs one more $11$.

**Step 3.** Multiply by $3 \times 11 = 33$: $1188 \times 33 = 39204 = 198^2$.

questions.stem_md: The LCM of two co-prime numbers is $391$. One of them is $17$. Find the other.
questions.solution_md: Co-prime numbers have HCF $1$, so $\text{LCM} = $ product. The other number is $\dfrac{391}{17} = 23$.

questions.stem_md: Express $4914$ as a product of its prime factors.

answer.model_answer_md: $4914 = 2 \times 2457 = 2 \times 3 \times 819 = 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 273 = 2 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 91 = 2 \times 3^3 \times 7 \times 13$.

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Divide by $2$: $2457$. **Step 2.** Divide by $3$ three times: $819$, $273$, $91$. **Step 3.** $91 = 7 \times 13$. So $4914 = 2 \times 3^3 \times 7 \times 13$. **Check:** $2 \times 27 \times 91 = 4914$.

questions.stem_md: Show that $5 \times 7 \times 9 \times 11 + 9$ is a composite number.

answer.model_answer_md:
$5 \times 7 \times 9 \times 11 + 9 = 9 \times (5 \times 7 \times 11 + 1) = 9 \times (385 + 1) = 9 \times 386 = 3474$.

It has the factor $9$ besides $1$ and itself (indeed $3474 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 193$), so it is composite.

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Take $9$ common. **Step 2.** The bracket is $386$, a natural number greater than $1$. **Step 3.** The number is $9 \times 386 = 3474$, a product of two factors each greater than $1$, so it is composite.

questions.stem_md: Can the number $35^n$, where $n$ is a natural number, end with the digit $0$? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: No. $35^n = (5 \times 7)^n = 5^n \times 7^n$. To end with $0$, a number must be divisible by $10 = 2 \times 5$, so $2$ must appear in its prime factorisation. By the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic the factorisation $5^n \times 7^n$ is unique and contains no $2$. So $35^n$ never ends with $0$ (it always ends with $5$).

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Factorise: $35^n = 5^n \times 7^n$. **Step 2.** Ending in $0$ needs the factor $2$. **Step 3.** Uniqueness of prime factorisation rules out any hidden factor $2$, so the answer is no.

marking_scheme.step: No factor 2, by uniqueness of factorisation, so cannot end in 0

questions.stem_md: Find the HCF and LCM of $132$ and $198$ by prime factorisation.

answer.model_answer_md:
$132 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 11$ and $198 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 11$.

HCF $= 2 \times 3 \times 11 = 66$. LCM $= 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 11 = 396$.

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Factorise both. **Step 2.** HCF: smaller power of each common prime, $66$. **Step 3.** LCM: greater power of every prime, $396$. **Check:** $66 \times 396 = 26136 = 132 \times 198$.

questions.stem_md: The HCF of two numbers is $23$ and their LCM is $1449$. If one of the numbers is $161$, find the other.

answer.model_answer_md:
For two numbers, $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = $ product. So the other number $= \dfrac{23 \times 1449}{161} = \dfrac{33327}{161} = 207$.

Check: $161 = 7 \times 23$, $207 = 3^2 \times 23$; HCF $= 23$, LCM $= 3^2 \times 7 \times 23 = 1449$. ✓

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** State and apply HCF × LCM = product. **Step 2.** Divide: $33327 \div 161 = 207$. **Step 3.** Verify with factorisations.

questions.stem_md: Both $5 + \sqrt{3}$ and $5 - \sqrt{3}$ are irrational. Work out their sum and their product. What do your answers show about adding or multiplying two irrational numbers?

answer.model_answer_md:
Sum: $(5 + \sqrt3) + (5 - \sqrt3) = 10$, which is rational.

Product: $(5 + \sqrt3)(5 - \sqrt3) = 25 - 3 = 22$, which is also rational.

So the sum, and the product, of two irrational numbers need **not** be irrational: here both are rational.

questions.solution_md: The $\sqrt3$ terms cancel in the sum; the product is a difference of squares, $a^2 - b^2$ with $a = 5$, $b = \sqrt3$.

marking_scheme.step: Conclusion: sum/product of irrationals can be rational

questions.stem_md: Meera says, "$\sqrt{8} + \sqrt{2}$ is rational, because $8 + 2 = 10$." Is she right? Justify your answer.

answer.model_answer_md:
No. Square roots do not add like that: $\sqrt8 + \sqrt2 \ne \sqrt{10}$, and in any case she has not taken any root.

$\sqrt8 = \sqrt{4 \times 2} = 2\sqrt2$, so $\sqrt8 + \sqrt2 = 2\sqrt2 + \sqrt2 = 3\sqrt2$.

$3\sqrt2$ is a non-zero rational number times the irrational $\sqrt2$, so it is **irrational**.

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Simplify $\sqrt8 = 2\sqrt2$. **Step 2.** Add like surds: $3\sqrt2$. **Step 3.** A non-zero rational times an irrational is irrational. Meera's reasoning adds the numbers under the roots, which is not allowed.

marking_scheme.step: Concludes irrational with reason; Meera wrong

questions.stem_md: Kabir claims that $\text{HCF}(18, 24, 36) \times \text{LCM}(18, 24, 36) = 18 \times 24 \times 36$. Check his claim.

answer.model_answer_md:
$18 = 2 \times 3^2$, $24 = 2^3 \times 3$, $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$.

HCF $= 2 \times 3 = 6$; LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^2 = 72$; $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 432$.

But $18 \times 24 \times 36 = 15552$. The claim is **false**: the product rule holds only for two numbers.

questions.solution_md: Compute both sides from the factorisations and compare: $432 \ne 15552$.

marking_scheme.step: Compares 432 with 15552 and rejects the claim

questions.stem_md: Riya writes: "$\text{HCF}(2^3 \times 5,\; 2 \times 3^2 \times 5) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$." Identify her mistake and find the correct HCF.

answer.model_answer_md:
Riya has taken the **greatest** power of **every** prime: that gives the LCM, $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$.

For the HCF take only the **common** primes, $2$ and $5$, with the **smaller** powers: HCF $= 2 \times 5 = 10$.

questions.solution_md: The numbers are $40$ and $90$. Common primes: $2$ (powers $3$ and $1$, take $1$) and $5$. $3$ is not common. HCF $= 10$, LCM $= 360$.

marking_scheme.step: Identifies that she found the LCM (greatest powers)

questions.stem_md: Find the HCF and LCM of $252$ and $375$ using prime factorisation, and verify that $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM}$ equals the product of the two numbers.

answer.model_answer_md:
$252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7$ and $375 = 3 \times 5^3$.

HCF $= 3$ (the only common prime, smaller power $3^1$).

LCM $= 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^3 \times 7 = 4 \times 9 \times 125 \times 7 = 31500$.

Verification: $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 3 \times 31500 = 94500$ and $252 \times 375 = 94500$. ✓

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Factorise. **Step 2.** HCF from common primes, LCM from all primes with greatest powers. **Step 3.** Multiply and compare: both sides are $94500$.

questions.stem_md: Three warning lamps on a factory floor flash every $36$, $48$ and $90$ seconds. They flash together at noon. Using prime factorisation, find after how many minutes they next flash together, and how many times they flash together in the next $2$ hours (not counting noon).

answer.model_answer_md:
$36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$, $48 = 2^4 \times 3$, $90 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5$.

LCM $= 2^4 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 720$ seconds $= 12$ minutes. They next flash together $12$ minutes after noon, at 12:12.

In $2$ hours $= 120$ minutes they flash together every $12$ minutes: $120 \div 12 = 10$ times.

questions.solution_md: "Together again" means a common multiple of all three intervals, and the first time is the LCM. Take every prime with its greatest power: $2^4$ from $48$, $3^2$ from $36$ or $90$, $5$ from $90$.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\sqrt{5}$ is irrational.

answer.model_answer_md:
Assume, to the contrary, that $\sqrt5$ is rational. Then $\sqrt5 = \dfrac ab$, where $a, b$ are co-prime integers and $b \ne 0$.

Squaring, $5b^2 = a^2$. So $5$ divides $a^2$, and since $5$ is prime, $5$ divides $a$. Write $a = 5c$ for some integer $c$.

Then $5b^2 = 25c^2$, so $b^2 = 5c^2$. Hence $5$ divides $b^2$, and so $5$ divides $b$.

Now $5$ divides both $a$ and $b$, which contradicts that $a$ and $b$ are co-prime. So our assumption is wrong, and $\sqrt5$ is irrational.

questions.solution_md: Proof by contradiction in four moves: assume $\dfrac ab$ in lowest terms; show $5 \mid a$; substitute $a = 5c$ to show $5 \mid b$; contradiction with co-prime.

marking_scheme.step: Assumption √5 = a/b with a, b co-prime

questions.stem_md: Given that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational, prove that $7 + 2\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

answer.model_answer_md:
Suppose $7 + 2\sqrt3 = r$, where $r$ is rational.

Then $2\sqrt3 = r - 7$, so $\sqrt3 = \dfrac{r - 7}{2}$.

Since $r$ is rational, $r - 7$ is rational and so is $\dfrac{r - 7}{2}$. This makes $\sqrt3$ rational, which contradicts the given fact.

Hence $7 + 2\sqrt3$ is irrational.

questions.solution_md: Isolate $\sqrt3$ using only operations that keep rational numbers rational (subtract $7$, divide by $2$).

questions.stem_md: Find the largest number that divides $398$, $436$ and $542$, leaving remainders $7$, $11$ and $15$ respectively.

answer.model_answer_md:
The number divides $398 - 7 = 391$, $436 - 11 = 425$ and $542 - 15 = 527$ exactly.

$391 = 17 \times 23$, $425 = 5^2 \times 17$, $527 = 17 \times 31$.

The largest such number is $\text{HCF} = 17$.

Check: $398 = 23 \times 17 + 7$, $436 = 25 \times 17 + 11$, $542 = 31 \times 17 + 15$. ✓

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Subtract the remainders. **Step 2.** Factorise. **Step 3.** HCF $= 17$, which is larger than every remainder, as a divisor must be.

questions.stem_md: Find the smallest four-digit number which leaves a remainder of $5$ when divided by each of $12$, $16$, $24$ and $36$.

answer.model_answer_md:
$12 = 2^2 \times 3$, $16 = 2^4$, $24 = 2^3 \times 3$, $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$, so $\text{LCM} = 2^4 \times 3^2 = 144$.

Numbers leaving remainder $5$ are $144k + 5$. The smallest four-digit multiple of $144$ is $144 \times 7 = 1008$ (since $144 \times 6 = 864$).

So the number is $1008 + 5 = 1013$.

questions.stem_md: Find the smallest perfect square that is divisible by each of $12$, $15$ and $20$.

answer.model_answer_md:
The number must be a multiple of $\text{LCM}(12, 15, 20)$. $12 = 2^2 \times 3$, $15 = 3 \times 5$, $20 = 2^2 \times 5$, so LCM $= 2^2 \times 3 \times 5 = 60$.

In a perfect square every exponent is even, so $3$ and $5$ each need one more factor: multiply $60$ by $3 \times 5 = 15$.

Smallest perfect square $= 60 \times 15 = 900 = 30^2$.

questions.solution_md: Every common multiple is a multiple of $60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$. Make the exponents of $3$ and $5$ even with the least extra factor $15$. **Check:** $900 \div 12 = 75$, $900 \div 15 = 60$, $900 \div 20 = 45$.

questions.stem_md: Prove that $\sqrt{3}$ is irrational. Hence prove that $2 + 5\sqrt{3}$ is irrational.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Part 1.** Assume $\sqrt3$ is rational: $\sqrt3 = \dfrac ab$ with $a, b$ co-prime integers, $b \ne 0$.

Squaring: $3b^2 = a^2$, so $3$ divides $a^2$. As $3$ is prime, $3$ divides $a$. Let $a = 3c$.

Then $3b^2 = 9c^2$, so $b^2 = 3c^2$; hence $3$ divides $b^2$ and therefore $3$ divides $b$.

So $3$ is a common factor of $a$ and $b$, contradicting that they are co-prime. Hence $\sqrt3$ is irrational.

**Part 2.** Suppose $2 + 5\sqrt3 = r$, rational. Then $\sqrt3 = \dfrac{r - 2}{5}$, which is rational because $r$ is rational. This contradicts Part 1. Hence $2 + 5\sqrt3$ is irrational.

questions.solution_md: Part 1 is the standard contradiction proof. Part 2 reuses Part 1: isolate $\sqrt3$ with operations (subtract $2$, divide by $5$) that keep rationals rational.

marking_scheme.step: Assumption √3 = a/b, a and b co-prime

questions.stem_md:
A school hall in Bhopal measures $15.12$ m by $10.8$ m. It is to be paved with identical square marble tiles, as large as possible, with no tile cut.

(a) Find the side of each tile.

(b) Find the number of tiles needed.

(c) If one tile costs ₹$180$, find the total cost of the tiles.

answer.model_answer_md:
Work in centimetres: $1512$ cm and $1080$ cm.

(a) $1512 = 2^3 \times 3^3 \times 7$ and $1080 = 2^3 \times 3^3 \times 5$. The largest tile side is the HCF $= 2^3 \times 3^3 = 216$ cm $= 2.16$ m.

(b) Tiles along the length $= \dfrac{1512}{216} = 7$; along the breadth $= \dfrac{1080}{216} = 5$. Number of tiles $= 7 \times 5 = 35$.

(c) Cost $= 35 \times 180 = $ ₹$6300$.

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** Convert to cm so both lengths are whole numbers. **Step 2.** Largest square tile dividing both sides: HCF. **Step 3.** Count tiles row by column. **Step 4.** Multiply by the price.

questions.stem_md:
Three friends jog on a circular track at a stadium in Kochi. Anil completes a lap in $252$ s, Bina in $308$ s and Charu in $198$ s. They start together from the same point and in the same direction.

(a) After how many minutes and seconds will they all be together at the starting point again?

(b) How many laps will each of them have completed by then?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $252 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7$, $308 = 2^2 \times 7 \times 11$, $198 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 11$.

LCM $= 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 7 \times 11 = 2772$ s $= 46$ min $12$ s.

(b) Anil: $\dfrac{2772}{252} = 11$ laps; Bina: $\dfrac{2772}{308} = 9$ laps; Charu: $\dfrac{2772}{198} = 14$ laps.

questions.solution_md: **Step 1.** "Together again at the start" is a common multiple of the lap times, and "first time" makes it the least one. **Step 2.** Factorise and take greatest powers. **Step 3.** $2772 = 46 \times 60 + 12$. **Step 4.** Divide by each lap time.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Find the HCF and LCM of $72$, $108$ and $180$ by prime factorisation.

(b) Show that the product of the HCF and LCM is **not** equal to the product of the three numbers, and find how many times larger the product of the numbers is.

(c) Explain, using exponents of primes, why the rule "HCF × LCM = product" works for two numbers but fails here.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $72 = 2^3 \times 3^2$, $108 = 2^2 \times 3^3$, $180 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5$.

HCF $= 2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$; LCM $= 2^3 \times 3^3 \times 5 = 1080$.

(b) $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = 36 \times 1080 = 38880$. Product $= 72 \times 108 \times 180 = 1399680$. These are not equal; $\dfrac{1399680}{38880} = 36$, so the product is $36$ times larger.

(c) For two numbers, each prime's exponents $m$ and $n$ appear once as the smaller (in the HCF) and once as the larger (in the LCM), and $\min(m, n) + \max(m, n) = m + n$, the exponent in the product. With three numbers the **middle** exponent is used by neither. For $2$: exponents $3, 2, 2$; HCF uses $2$, LCM uses $3$, total $5$, but the product has $7$. For $3$: $2 + 3 = 5$ against $7$. For $5$: $0 + 1 = 1$ against $1$. The missing $2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$ is exactly the factor found in (b).

questions.solution_md: Compare exponents prime by prime. The "lost" middle exponents ($2^2$ and $3^2$) multiply to $36$, matching the ratio in (b).

marking_scheme.step: Two-number reason: min + max = sum of exponents

questions.stem_md:
(a) A student "proves" that $\sqrt{4}$ is irrational as follows.

*Let $\sqrt4 = \dfrac ab$, with $a, b$ co-prime. Then $4b^2 = a^2$, so $4$ divides $a^2$, so $4$ divides $a$. Let $a = 4c$. Then $4b^2 = 16c^2$, so $b^2 = 4c^2$, so $4$ divides $b$. This contradicts co-primality, so $\sqrt4$ is irrational.*

Identify the incorrect step, give a counter-example to it, and state the truth about $\sqrt4$.

(b) Prove that $\sqrt{6}$ is irrational.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The wrong step is "$4$ divides $a^2$, so $4$ divides $a$". This rule holds only when the divisor is **prime**, and $4$ is not prime. Counter-example: $4$ divides $6^2 = 36$, but $4$ does not divide $6$. In fact $\sqrt4 = 2 = \dfrac21$, which is rational.

(b) Assume $\sqrt6 = \dfrac ab$ with $a, b$ co-prime, $b \ne 0$. Then $6b^2 = a^2$. So $2$ divides $a^2$; as $2$ is prime, $2$ divides $a$. Let $a = 2c$. Then $6b^2 = 4c^2$, so $3b^2 = 2c^2$. Hence $2$ divides $3b^2$; since $2$ does not divide $3$, $2$ divides $b^2$, and so $2$ divides $b$. Now $2$ divides both $a$ and $b$, a contradiction. So $\sqrt6$ is irrational.

questions.solution_md: (a) The lemma "$p \mid a^2 \Rightarrow p \mid a$" needs $p$ prime; with $4$ it fails, e.g. $a = 6$. (b) Work with the prime $2$ (or $3$) dividing $6$, not with $6$ itself.

questions.stem_md: Two natural numbers have HCF $16$ and LCM $960$. Find **all** possible pairs of such numbers. Explain your method.

answer.model_answer_md:
Since the HCF is $16$, write the numbers as $16m$ and $16n$, where $m$ and $n$ are co-prime (otherwise the HCF would be larger).

Then $\text{LCM} = 16mn = 960$, so $mn = 60$.

Co-prime pairs $(m, n)$ with $m \le n$ and $mn = 60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 5$: the factor $2^2$ must stay together, so the pairs are $(1, 60)$, $(3, 20)$, $(4, 15)$, $(5, 12)$. ($(2, 30)$ and $(6, 10)$ are not co-prime.)

The pairs of numbers are $(16, 960)$, $(48, 320)$, $(64, 240)$ and $(80, 192)$.

questions.solution_md: Check one pair: $64 = 2^6$, $240 = 2^4 \times 3 \times 5$; HCF $= 2^4 = 16$ and LCM $= 2^6 \times 3 \times 5 = 960$. ✓ Each pair also satisfies $16 \times 960 = 15360 = $ product.

marking_scheme.step: Writes numbers as 16m, 16n with m, n co-prime
Verification of at least one pair

questions.passage_md: At the Esplanade bus depot in Kolkata, three city routes start at 6:00 a.m. Buses on route A leave every $15$ minutes, on route B every $20$ minutes and on route C every $36$ minutes. The depot manager wants to know when buses on all three routes leave at the same time, so she can post an extra inspector at those moments. The depot runs until 9:00 p.m.

children.stem_md: Which idea gives the first time after 6:00 a.m. when buses on all three routes leave together?
children.solution_md: Departures of each route are multiples of its interval; a common departure is a common multiple, and the first one is the least common multiple.

children.stem_md: After how many minutes from 6:00 a.m. do all three routes next leave together?
**(i)** After 6:00 a.m., how many more times do all three routes leave together, up to and including 9:00 p.m.?

answer.model_answer_md: 6:00 a.m. to 9:00 p.m. is $900$ minutes. Common departures every $180$ minutes: $\dfrac{900}{180} = 5$ more times — 9 a.m., 12 noon, 3 p.m., 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.

children.solution_md: Duration $900$ min; divide by the LCM $180$.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** If route C changes to a bus every 24 minutes, at what time after 6:00 a.m. will all three routes first leave together?

answer.model_answer_md: $24 = 2^3 \times 3$. New LCM $= \text{LCM}(15, 20, 24) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120$ minutes, so at 8:00 a.m.

questions.passage_md: Farida runs a bangle shop in Jaipur's Johari Bazaar. Before Teej she has $432$ red bangles, $576$ green bangles and $720$ golden bangles. She wants to pack them in identical packets so that every packet has the **same number** of bangles, each packet has bangles of **only one colour**, and she uses the **fewest** packets possible.

children.stem_md: The number of bangles in each packet should be

options.text_md: any common factor of the three numbers
the product of the three numbers

children.solution_md: The packet size must divide all three counts (common factor), and the fewest packets needs the largest such size: the HCF. Any common factor works, but only the HCF gives the fewest packets.

children.stem_md: How many bangles go in each packet?
**(i)** How many packets does Farida make in all?

answer.model_answer_md: Red: $\dfrac{432}{144} = 3$, green: $\dfrac{576}{144} = 4$, golden: $\dfrac{720}{144} = 5$. Total $= 12$ packets.

children.solution_md: Divide each count by 144 and add.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Her assistant suggests packets of 48 bangles instead. Find how many packets this needs, and say why 48 is allowed but not the best choice.

answer.model_answer_md: $\dfrac{432}{48} + \dfrac{576}{48} + \dfrac{720}{48} = 9 + 12 + 15 = 36$ packets. $48$ divides all three counts, so it is a common factor, but it is smaller than the HCF $144$, so it needs three times as many packets.

alternatives.solution_md: 48 is a common factor (48 divides 144), not the highest.

Or (ii) $\text{LCM}(1, 2, \dots, 10) = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520$: the highest powers needed are $2^3$ (from $8$), $3^2$ (from $9$), $5$ and $7$.

questions.solution_md: (a) Primes $2, 3, 5, 7$. (b) $2520k$ is a perfect square when every exponent is even: $2^3 \to$ needs $2$, $3^2$ fine, $5 \to$ needs $5$, $7 \to$ needs $7$; $k = 2 \times 5 \times 7 = 70$, and $2520 \times 70 = 176400 = 420^2$. (c) See model answer.
questions.passage_md: In a maths club meeting in Lucknow, the teacher writes on the board: $2520 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$. Arjun says, "I have found a different prime factorisation: $2520 = 4 \times 630$." Sana adds that $2520$ is special: it is the smallest number divisible by every whole number from $1$ to $10$.

children.stem_md: How many distinct prime factors does 2520 have?
children.solution_md: The distinct primes are $2, 3, 5, 7$: four. (Counting with repetition gives $3 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7$, option (b).)

children.stem_md: The smallest natural number $k$ for which $2520k$ is a perfect square is ___.
children.solution_md: $2520 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$. Make every exponent even: multiply by $2 \times 5 \times 7 = 70$. Check: $2520 \times 70 = 176400 = 420^2$.

children.stem_md: **(i)** Is Arjun right? Explain using the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

answer.model_answer_md: No. A prime factorisation must use only primes, and $4$ and $630$ are composite. Breaking them down, $4 = 2^2$ and $630 = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$, gives $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7$ again. The Fundamental Theorem says the prime factorisation is unique apart from order, so there is no "different" one.

children.solution_md: Reduce 4 × 630 to primes; it matches the board.

marking_scheme.step: Reduces to the same factorisation; uniqueness stated

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** Use prime factorisation to justify Sana's statement that 2520 is the smallest number divisible by every whole number from 1 to 10.

answer.model_answer_md: The smallest such number is $\text{LCM}(1, 2, \dots, 10)$. The greatest prime powers among $1$ to $10$ are $2^3$ (from $8$), $3^2$ (from $9$), $5$ and $7$. So the LCM is $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 = 2520$.

alternatives.solution_md: LCM takes the greatest power of each prime up to 10.

answer.model_answer_md: Suppose $3 + \sqrt2 = r$ for a rational $r$. Then $\sqrt2 = r - 3$. A difference of two rationals is rational, so $\sqrt2$ would be rational — a contradiction. Hence $P$ is irrational.

questions.passage_md: A farmer near Nashik is fencing three sides of his vineyard along a road. The sides measure $396$ m, $504$ m and $612$ m, and they meet end to end at two corners. He wants concrete poles at **equal** distances along all three sides, with a pole at every corner and at both ends, and the distance between poles as **large** as possible (a whole number of metres).

children.stem_md: The largest possible distance between poles is

options.text_md: the sum of the three sides divided by 3
the HCF of the three sides
the LCM of the three sides

children.solution_md: Each side must be an exact number of gaps, so the gap divides every side; the largest such gap is the HCF.

children.stem_md: Find the distance between consecutive poles, in metres.
**(i)** How many poles are needed in all?

answer.model_answer_md: Gaps: $\dfrac{396}{36} + \dfrac{504}{36} + \dfrac{612}{36} = 11 + 14 + 17 = 42$. The fence is an open path, so poles $= 42 + 1 = 43$ (corner poles are shared, not double-counted).

children.solution_md: Count gaps, then add one pole for an open path.

alternatives.stem_md: **(ii)** The supplier can only deliver wire in pieces shorter than 20 m, so each gap must be less than 20 m. What is now the largest possible gap? Explain.

alternatives.solution_md: Common divisors are exactly the divisors of the HCF.
